blocks.text: Add behavior to an object by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface and delegates to it.

A **decorator** holds a reference to a component of the same type, forwards each call, and adds work before or after. Because the wrapper is itself a component, wrappers **stack** in any order and combination, chosen at runtime, without a subclass for every combination.

items: **Varies:** which responsibilities are added, and in what order.
**Stays stable:** the component interface and the wrapped class.
**Chosen by:** the code that assembles the stack, often at startup.

blocks.text: A decorator and the object it wraps are interchangeable to the client. If the wrapper changes the interface, that is an Adapter.

walkthrough.note: The component interface that both the real object and every wrapper implement.
The concrete component does the base work and knows nothing about decorators.
An abstract decorator holds the wrapped `Notifier` and is itself a `Notifier`. It holds the shared `next` field, so each concrete wrapper writes only its own concern.
Each wrapper adds exactly one concern and then calls `next`. `Prefixed` changes the argument; `Audited` records it.
The stack is assembled by nesting constructors. The outermost wrapper runs first; swap the order and the behavior changes.
The client holds a plain `Notifier`. It cannot tell, and does not need to know, how many wrappers sit behind it.

blocks.text: Resilience layers around an outbound HTTP client.

A payments client needs auth headers, metrics, retries and a circuit breaker, but a batch job wants only metrics and retries, and tests want none. Each concern is a decorator around `HttpGateway`. Production composes all of them; each environment picks its own stack in one place and the callers never change.
Payoff: concerns are written and tested once, in isolation, and combined by assembly rather than by subclassing.

lists.title: Use when
items: Optional behaviors must combine freely at runtime.
Subclassing would explode into one class per combination.
You cannot modify the wrapped class, or should not.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The behavior is always on: put it in the class.
The interface is wide; every wrapper must forward every method.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Order matters: a retry outside versus inside a timeout behaves differently.
Identity checks and `instanceof` see the wrapper, not the real object.
Stack traces and debugging get deep, and wide interfaces drift when a method is forgotten.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Five wrappers that always appear together: merge them into one class.
A decorator that quietly changes the contract, such as swallowing exceptions.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: For a single-method interface, a higher-order function can wrap behavior without a class per layer.
`java.lang.reflect.Proxy` can generate forwarding wrappers for wide interfaces.

rows.difference: Same wrapping shape, different intent. A proxy controls access to its subject and may manage its lifecycle; a decorator adds responsibilities that the client opts into and can stack.
An adapter changes the interface to fit a caller. A decorator keeps the interface identical and changes the behavior.
Composite holds many children and aggregates their results; a decorator wraps exactly one component and augments it.
Strategy swaps the internals of an object through a hook it exposes. Decorator wraps from the outside and needs no hook.
A decorator always delegates and adds. A chain handler may stop the request and answer it itself.

entries.name: ForwardingList
entries.detail: A forwarding base class for decorating a `List`; override only the methods you change.

options.why: The wrapper has the same interface as what it wraps, adds one behavior, delegates, and stacks with other wrappers.
A proxy controls access to one subject, for example by laziness or permissions. These wrappers add behavior and stack freely.
The interface is the same on both sides, so nothing is being adapted.
Each wrapper holds exactly one `Sink`, not a group of children whose results are combined.

exercises.scenario: An HTTP client class is used by dozens of services. Some need logging, some need retries, some need auth headers, and a few need all three, in a specific order. The class is in a vendor library and cannot be changed.

options.why: Wrappers implementing the same interface can be stacked per service in any combination, without touching the vendor class.
It swaps one algorithm, but here several independent concerns must layer on top of the same call.
Needs subclasses of a class you cannot change, and yields a class per combination.
The interface already fits callers; only behavior needs to be added.

exercises.explanation: The wrapper ignores the component it was given and writes to a hard-coded sink, so anything stacked beneath it is bypassed. Delegate with `inner.write(out)`.

template: class ConsoleSink implements Sink { public void write(String l) { System.out.println(l); } }

exercises.prompt: Order the lines so that each one only uses what came before.
exercises.explanation: A decorator needs the component it wraps, so the stack is built from the innermost object outward, and calls go to the outermost wrapper.

template: record FileSink(Path p) implements Sink { public void write(String l) {} }
record Masked(Sink in) implements Sink { public void write(String l) { in.write(l); } }
record Timestamped(Sink in) implements Sink { public void write(String l) { in.write(l); } }

exercises.prompt: Explain Decorator in your own words: why does it keep the same interface, and how does it differ from Proxy?

modelAnswer.text: A decorator wraps a component that has the same interface and adds behavior before or after delegating. Because the wrapper is itself a component, wrappers stack in any order, avoiding a subclass per combination. A proxy looks the same but controls access to its subject, such as lazily creating it or checking permissions, rather than adding stackable features.

keyPoints: Same interface as the wrapped component, so it is transparent
Delegates, adding behavior before or after
Stacks at runtime in any order; avoids subclass explosion
Proxy controls access and lifecycle; decorator adds responsibilities
